extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity officers, and readers interested in publication ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the grounds, processes, and responsibilities that lead to expressions of concern, institutional investigations, and journal retractions in clinical research (e.g., fabrication, plagiarism, lack of IRB approval). Intended to guide editors, institutions, and the research community in detecting and responding to misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics committee / IRB approval required
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical studies must have ethics committee (IRB) approval; publications lacking such approval do not "conform to the global standard of ethics for clinical studies." (Toho University: "Eight of the nine clinical studies were conducted without any ethics committee’s approval...should be retracted since they did not conform to the global standard of ethics for clinical studies.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should request and verify copies of ethical approval documents when concerns arise. Lack of documented approval is sufficient grounds for retraction of affected clinical-study publications and may trigger institutional disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of data fabrication or falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: Data that are shown to be fabricated or falsified (editors were "informed that not only were the data fabricated, but that Fujii had not obtained approval to conduct such a study").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evidence indicates fabrication/falsification, journals should coordinate with the author’s institution and consider retraction. Institutions should investigate and impose appropriate disciplinary measures (e.g., dismissal). Editors may issue expressions of concern while investigations proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism as a trigger for investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission containing apparent plagiarism can trigger an institutional or editorial investigation ("The investigation was triggered last spring when Fujii submitted a manuscript to the journal containing what appeared to be plagiarism.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plagiarism detection on submission should prompt editorial queries and possible investigation; if substantiated, it can be cause for rejection, retraction of published work, and further institutional inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical anomalies / 'incredibly nice' data as red flags
rubrics_metrics.description: Unusually consistent or improbably favorable results (Kranke et al.: "results reported by Fujii et al. are incredibly nice" and Apfel: "The likelihood that the data are true...less than one seven in a billion").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reviewers should flag and investigate statistical improbabilities (identical side-effect rates across groups, effect sizes far outside norms). Statistical review, requests for raw data, and independent reanalysis are appropriate responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal editorial due diligence and follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors are expected to perform due diligence when concerns arise: analyze statistics, request ethical approval forms, correspond with institutions, and, if needed, issue expressions of concern or retractions (Shafer: "agreed to analyze the statistics...asked for a copy of the ethical approval form...will be posting a letter to readers...issue expressions of concern").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should proactively investigate credible allegations, request documentation, consult statistical experts, and publicly communicate actions (expressions of concern, corrections, or retractions). Continuing to publish related manuscripts while allegations remain unresolved is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional investigation and disciplinary action
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should organize investigation committees, make searching inquiries into credibility, request explanations from authors/co-authors, and impose disciplinary decisions where warranted (Toho University organized a committee, asked for explanations, and decided disciplinary dismissal was appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities and hospitals must investigate allegations, determine which publications are affected, notify journals/publishers, and publicly report findings and sanctions where appropriate. Institutional findings often drive retractions and corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction grounds and process
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications may be retracted for multiple reasons including lack of ethics approval, data fabrication, plagiarism, or redundant/duplicate data (examples throughout the article and related cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction decisions should be based on evidence (institutional findings, editorial investigations, statistical analyses). Journals should coordinate with publishers and, where possible, provide clear notices summarizing reasons for retraction and the extent (number of affected papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and clear communication about investigations/retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions and journals should clearly report which papers are affected and the basis for retractions; incomplete statements hinder clarity (Toho University posted a statement but "there’s no list on the page" and claims about who requested retractions were unclear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed public statements naming affected publications and reasons for action. Clarify whether authors requested retraction or whether the institution/journal initiated it to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of clinical impact of problematic research
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether suspect findings influenced clinical practice (Apfel: "If Fujii’s data had an impact, people would have used 3 mg. But people didn’t.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When misconduct is identified in clinical research, assess whether patient care or regulatory decisions were affected and notify relevant clinical bodies/regulators as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness of regulators, societies, and journals to concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders (regulators, professional societies, journals) should respond to credible concerns, but may sometimes fail to do so (Apfel wrote to FDA and Japanese counterpart and received little or no reply).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise concerns with multiple appropriate bodies (journals, institutions, regulators, professional societies) and document communications; persistent non-response should be escalated and publicly noted where appropriate to encourage accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external critique and meta-analysis to detect anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: External analysis (letters, meta-analyses) can reveal inconsistencies across a body of work (Apfel, Kranke et al. analyzed Fujii’s trials and found efficacy estimates far outside other groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage and pay attention to post-publication critiques, letters, and meta-analyses as tools to detect systematic anomalies; journals should act on robust external evidence and consider re-reviewing implicated studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid publishing further work while allegations are unresolved
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuing to publish an author’s additional manuscripts while prior allegations of impropriety remain unresolved is inappropriate (Shafer: "It was similarly inappropriate to publish additional manuscripts by Fujii when the allegations of fraud were unresolved.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should consider pausing acceptance/publication of submissions from authors under credible investigation until issues are resolved or corrective measures are in place.
